title: Paired horns of ruminants are conjugate, mirror-image spirals

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Paired horns of ruminants are conjugate, mirror-image spirals

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The paired horns of hollow-horned ruminants are conjugate spirals, the left horn being the mirror image of the right.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But the two horns are in symmetry one with another; they form “conjugate” spirals, one being the “mirror-image” of the other.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIII, “The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion”; topic “Hollow horns of ruminants”. Scope: sheep, goats, oxen and antelopes (Bovidae)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch13-02: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.84

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Mirror symmetry has a direct, decisive geometric test requiring only paired specimens. Public museum media provide broad enough coverage to resolve the generalization for many bovid groups.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reflect one horn of each paired 3D specimen and quantify registration error against its mate, comparing observed symmetry with within-individual shape variation. Low residual asymmetry supports conjugate mirror-image spirals; systematic same-handedness or major nonmirror geometry refutes the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Damage and pose differences can inflate asymmetry.

Some records show detached single horns rather than pairs.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.88
data existence: 0.75
discriminating power: 0.95
operationalizability: 0.96
data adequacy: 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Bilateral mirror symmetry of a pair of horns is a routine landmark or surface comparison, and open cranial scans already include both sides of many bovid skulls. The sample is not a complete survey of every genus, but it is large enough to confirm the general rule or to expose a repeated exception. Wear, injury, and core-versus-sheath differences are measurable nuisances, not barriers to the test.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reflect one horn of a bovid skull onto the other and measure the residual after alignment. Mirror symmetry is confirmed if residuals are within scanning and wear error across sheep, goats, oxen, and antelopes; a systematic directional asymmetry shared by many species would refute the conjugate-spiral claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Museum holdings over-represent domestic cattle, sheep, and a few hunted antelopes.

Scans more often preserve bony cores than the keratin sheath, and the sheath carries much of the visible spiral.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: In hollow-horned ruminants (Bovidae) the two horns of a pair are conjugate spirals: each is a helico-spiral of the same length, curvature and pitch as its partner but of opposite handedness, so that reflecting one horn in the skull's sagittal plane reproduces the other.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: fetch.py queries the MorphoSource public API for bovid media (10 taxon and part searches), writes every bovid record with its visibility, file size and use-agreement type to derived/candidate_media.csv, and then tries three download routes for the two largest open crania. The API itself answers normally; every download route fails (HTTP 404 for the API download path, and an Anubis 'Access Denied' page for the web download and media pages, also when retried through a headless Chrome browser). MorphoSource downloads additionally require a logged-in account that accepts the specimen's use agreement, which this run must not create. No mesh was obtained, so there is nothing to analyse and no analysis.py.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered (claim supported). For at least 8 bovid crania from public 3D scans spanning at least 4 genera, extract the midline curve of each horn core from the mesh, fit a helico-spiral (constant curvature and torsion in the Frenet sense, i.e. a conical helix) to each, and compare the pair: in at least 80% of specimens the signs of the torsion of the left and right horn are opposite, and the magnitudes of length, mean curvature and mean torsion agree within 15% (|L - R| / mean of the pair).

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered (claim refuted). In more than 20% of specimens the two horns have torsion of the same sign (both horns coiling the same way, i.e. not conjugate), or the paired magnitudes differ by more than 15% in more than 20% of specimens beyond what the same measurement applied twice to one horn reproduces. If fewer than 8 specimens or fewer than 4 genera can be obtained from public sources without authentication, the verdict is 'inconclusive' with reason 'data-unavailable'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: bovid crania with both horn cores actually obtained (0 of 13 open candidates)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson's 'conjugate' means mirror-image, i.e. enantiomorphic: his point is that the two horns are not two copies of one spiral but a left-handed and a right-handed version of the same spiral. The operational quantity is therefore the sign of the torsion (handedness) of each horn's midline, plus the magnitudes of its length, curvature and torsion. Horn cores (bone) rather than sheaths are used because that is what 3D scans of museum crania show; sheath and core differ in length and tip curvature but not in handedness. Asymmetry from injury, wear or captivity is expected in a minority of specimens, hence the 80% threshold. Candidate sources, in order: MorphoSource media with open visibility (bovid crania and horn cores), other public 3D specimen repositories, and any dataset giving paired left/right horn geometry. No specimen measurement has been inspected before this pre-registration; only catalogue hit counts, visibility flags and HTTP status codes.

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The specimens needed exist and are catalogued: 44 bovid cranium or skull media on MorphoSource, 13 of them flagged 'open' visibility, spanning 6 genera (Ammotragus, Bison, Capra, Oryx, Ovis, Qurliqnoria). What failed is access: every download route returns an Anubis bot-protection page or HTTP 404 from this host, and MorphoSource downloads require an authenticated account that accepts each specimen's use agreement. Under the pre-registered rule ('fewer than 8 specimens or 4 genera obtainable without authentication') the verdict is inconclusive, not a judgement on the claim.

Measurement datasets about bovid horns do exist (Dryad: ontogenetic allometry of horn length; horn investment in female bovids), but they record one horn length per individual or species means, so they cannot address left-versus-right mirror symmetry at all.

With an account the test as pre-registered looks tractable: the open candidates include Bison bison (15.8 MB mesh), Bison priscus, Ovis ammon polii, Capra ibex, Ammotragus lervia and Oryx gazella CT series, which would give 4-6 genera, short of the pre-registered 8 specimens unless the restricted-download items are added.

Horn cores, not sheaths, are what these scans show; Thompson's figures are of sheaths. Handedness is the same in core and sheath, but the quantitative comparison (length, curvature, torsion) would differ between the two, which the pre-registered thresholds do not account for.
